problem: Existing visual navigation policies (ViNT, NoMaD, LeLaN) are trained in simulation, indoors or on small robot datasets and need precise goals (coordinates or images). They cannot follow free-form language in real urban scenes, and teleoperated urban data is scarce and costly.
motivation: Last-mile delivery robots need to follow ambiguous, landmark-based instructions in unfamiliar cities. Web-scale city walking videos are abundant but have no action or language labels, and many clips are unsuitable for robots (head-turn viewpoint divergence, dense crowds). The paper therefore builds an automatic labeling and filtering pipeline to turn them into imitation-learning data.
key_idea: Convert 2,000+ hours of YouTube walking videos into 1,566 hours of robot-compatible trajectories with VLM-generated landmark instructions (3M triplets), then train a FiLM-conditioned Transformer waypoint policy on them.
insight: Data quality and scale drive the gains. Web pre-training lifts real-world success from 33.4% (UrbanNav*, real data only) to 83.3%, and the noisy-instruction success rate from 25.0 to 87.5. Error falls steadily from 300 to 1,500 hours and plateaus near 1,200 hours. In the ablation, removing FiLM hurts most (AOE 9.22 to 11.35), and the feature-hallucination loss helps only with the filtered, clean data (AOE 9.56 to 9.22 with it).
method: Trajectory annotation: split videos into 2-minute clips and run DPVO visual odometry for per-frame camera poses in a local frame; 106,603 trajectories (3,553 h). Short 8-step windows limit the effect of VO drift.

Robot-compatible filtering: reject clips with pitch variation over 15°, clips whose movement-vs-view direction diverges by over 60° in a sliding window, and clips where YOLOv10 finds more than 5 people in a frame in more than 3 frames; 47,008 trajectories (1,566 h) remain.

Landmark and instruction annotation: Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects static landmarks near the path (boxes and names) and generates concise instructions; low-confidence annotations are manually filtered. This gives 3M annotations, ~65 landmarks per trajectory and ~17 words per description.

Policy architecture: frozen CLIP encodes the instruction and frozen DINOv2 encodes frames. FiLM modulates the current-frame embedding by the language feature. A Transformer encoder over all tokens (8 past frames) outputs 8 future waypoints via a lightweight head, plus direction and arrival predictions.
Loss: L2 waypoint regression, negative-cosine orientation loss, BCE arrival loss, and L1 future-feature hallucination loss, combined as a weighted sum.
Training sampling: pick a random landmark as the goal, sample the start 10-60 frames before the goal time, and sample steps very near the goal as arrival positives.

setting.backbone: Frozen CLIP text encoder + frozen DINOv2 visual encoder, plus a trained FiLM + Transformer encoder policy with an action head
setting.training_data: 1,566 h / 47,008 filtered YouTube walking trajectories with 3M VLM-generated instruction-landmark labels (Qwen2.5-VL-72B annotator); fine-tuned with a small amount of real-world robot data (amount unspecified)
setting.observation: egocentric monocular RGB, current frame + 8 past frames, plus a language instruction
setting.action_space: predicted egocentric waypoints (next 8 steps), plus arrival flag
setting.simulator: real world only (offline evaluation on held-out web-video data; real robot deployment)

results: On the offline benchmark, UrbanNav beats LeLaN on all metrics, e.g. unseen AOE 9.22 vs 10.36 and ADE 0.88 vs 0.98. In real-robot tests it reaches 83.3% success vs 62.5% for the best baseline, LeLaN, and 87.5% under noisy instructions vs 62.5% for LeLaN.
limitations: Designed for local navigation: it cannot explore for targets that are initially out of view (62.5% SR in obstructed cases).
Real-world evaluation is small, and success falls at night (75.0%). Offline metrics only compare to ground-truth trajectories rather than end-to-end task completion.
VO-based pose labels are noisy and drift, and the landmark annotation needs manual filtering.
